title: Visit the Nodes Level by Level

concept.title: Breadth-first search visits the nodes in order of their distance from the start
body: *Breadth-first search* (BFS) starts at one node, visits all its neighbours, then all the neighbours of those neighbours, and so on: it explores the graph **in rings** around the start. It is done with a **queue**: take the node at the front, and put its unvisited neighbours at the back.

To make the visiting order unique, the neighbours of a node are taken **in increasing order of their numbers**: sort every neighbour list once after building it. A node is marked as seen **when it is put in the queue**, not when it is taken out, so that it enters the queue only once.

The order in which nodes enter the queue is the BFS order, and it has a very useful property: the **distance** (number of edges) from the start never goes down along it. That is why BFS finds shortest paths in graphs without weights, which the next tasks use.

statement: An undirected graph has `n` nodes and `m` edges. Do a breadth-first search from node 1 in which the neighbours of a node are taken in increasing order. Print the nodes in the order in which they are visited (only the nodes that can be reached from node 1).
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n) and the number of edges.
Each of the next `m` lines has two numbers `u` and `v`: an edge between the nodes `u` and `v`.
outputFormat: The visited nodes in order on one line.
constraints: There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.

examples.note: Node 1 first, then its neighbours 2 and 3, then the new neighbours of 2 (node 5) and of 3 (node 4): 1 2 3 5 4. Node 6 is not reachable.

hints: Sort the neighbour list of every node.
Use a queue that starts with node 1 and mark nodes as seen when they enter the queue.
The order in which nodes enter the queue is the answer.

explanation: The neighbour lists are sorted; a queue starting with node 1 takes the nodes in front-to-back order and appends the unseen neighbours of each. The queue is the visiting order.
solution.complexity: Time O(n + m log m), space O(n + m).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
edges = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

adj = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v)
    adj[v].append(u)
for lst in adj:
    lst.sort()
seen = [False] * (n + 1)
seen[1] = True
order = [1]
for v in order:
    for w in adj[v]:
        if not seen[w]:
            seen[w] = True
            order.append(w)
print(*order)
